findings: Study 1: the Earth-GNSS orbit determination in the NRHO is weak: mean tracked satellites 0.92, at least one at 62 % of epochs, four or more at none, position sigma about 351 m; ground OD about 23 m. The two covariances are mutually consistent (C1, C2) but the GNSS covariance is too wide to expose a 10 m model error (C3).

Study 2: at the registered 12 dBi the double-difference problem is not formable (two or more common satellites at 85 of 433 epochs, three or more at none). At the amended 25 dBi integer fixing is still not reached: Monte Carlo success 1 to 3 %, though the float orbiter sigma falls from 45.6 m (1 day) to 6.3 m (3 days) and the fixed one from 18.5 m to 2.1 m.
Study 3: orbiter links raise the smallest information eigenvalue about 111-fold and cut the CRLB trace to about 1 %, conditional on the orbit being known in the lunar axes.

Study 4: with the registered technique sigmas the laser-versus-GNSS translation is limited by measurement noise (about 1 m), not by the 1 mm local tie; the local tie sets the floor only for near-perfect techniques (T2).
Study 5: the family-by-family information is in the report; the orbiter k2 sensitivity is an upper-end figure.
disclosures: Moon occultation of the Earth-GNSS signals was added to the study-1 link rule after the first run; it changed no number.
Amendment 1 (study-2 default 25 dBi, availability counts only seen) and amendment 2 (study-2 trials 2000 -> 400 and the surface-longitude convention fix) are in PREREGISTRATION-amendment-1.md.

The first T2 scoring used a normal-equation inversion and missed (1.3 % at a 0.1 m tie, values below the floor at 1 m, which is impossible). The cause was conditioning; the covariance moved to the square-root route (fim::crlb_srif) and T2 was rescored with the same bar.

The scored carrier-phase configuration (three arcs, 400 draws, about eight minutes) is scenarios/carrier-phase-scored.toml here; its result is stored as tests/fixtures/lunar_infra/phase_full_run.json. The shipped example is a quick two-arc, ten-draw run of the same study.
